evidence.title: A community-codesigned LLM-powered chatbot for primary care: a randomized controlled trial
evidence.effect: improved to 2.95 with e-learning vs 2.34 without
evidence.quote: The primary outcome was the objective awareness of health needs assessed through patient dialogues with P&P Care and was significantly higher in the e-learning plus group (2.95 ± 1.22) than in the consultation-only group (2.34 ± 1.02; P < 0.001; Fig. 3a ).

evidence.title: Evaluating Evidence-Based Communication through Generative AI using a Cross-Sectional Study with Laypeople Seeking Screening Information
evidence.effect: Simple boost improved response quality, though it remained below optimal standards.
evidence.quote: Study 2 revealed that laypeople frequently generated poor-quality responses; however, a simple boost improved response quality, though it remained below optimal standards.

evidence.title: Evaluating evidence-based health information from generative AI using a cross-sectional study with laypeople seeking screening information
evidence.outcome: Evidence-based response quality after prompting boost
evidence.effect: Improved quality: MAPPinfo F(1,294)=15.26, p<0.001, ηp²=0.05; ebmNucleus F(1,294)=12.12, p=0.001, ηp²=0.04.
evidence.quote: The boosting intervention for more informed prompting moderately improved the quality of elicited health information across all LLMs (Fig. 2a–c ), as indicated by ANOVA main effects for MAPPinfo ( F (1,294) = 15.26, p < 0.001, η p 2 = 0 . 05 ) and ebmNucleus ( F (1,294) = 12.12, p = 0.001, η p 2 = 0 . 04 ).

commentary.bottom_line: Three randomized trials suggest that user instruction may improve how people use AI tools, but they measured response quality and health awareness rather than safe-use outcomes, and none tested instructions for mental health chatbots. The case for this recommendation rests mainly on FDA labeling expectations, a Utah statute, and expert commentary.

perspectives.view: Three randomized trials test forms of user instruction. A deployed trial of 2,113 participants in China reported awareness scores of 2.95 with e-learning versus 2.34 without. Two simulated trials of 300 participants each found that prompting boosts improved response quality, and one reported quality still below optimal. Indirect outcomes and settings lower certainty to low.

The two simulated trials measured the quality of chatbot answers after users received prompting guidance. They did not measure harms, crisis recognition, or whether users stayed within safe-use limits. Better answers may lower some risk. No supplied study shows that instructions or disclaimers stop misuse before it reaches a patient.

Only the China trial took place in a real deployment, and it delivered structured e-learning rather than brief on-screen directions. The simulated trials used short prompting boosts, which suggests that light-touch guidance can shift user behavior. They did not report how often users read or retained the instructions in routine use.

The China trial enrolled rural, older, low-literacy, and non-English-speaking participants and found higher awareness scores with e-learning. This suggests that instruction can reach groups with fewer resources. The results may not carry over to American Medicaid or safety-net patients, who differ in language, health system, and access to technology.

FDA draft guidance says device manufacturers are required to provide labeling with adequate directions for use. Utah HB 452 requires mental health chatbots to put user safety ahead of engagement metrics. These sources create obligations for AI tools that qualify as devices and for chatbots in Utah. Neither source cites trial evidence on whether instructions work.

Commentators ask that users understand what a chatbot can and cannot do and be told to seek human help when in distress. The supplied trials did not test disclaimers or referral to a human. Whether instructions help a distressed person reach care remains untested.

commentary.research_gap: No supplied trial tested safe-use instructions or disclaimers for mental health chatbots, and none measured misuse, missed crises, harm, or contact with a human clinician. No study documenting the hazard was supplied. Trials in clinical deployments in the United States should compare instruction formats against safety outcomes rather than response quality alone.
commentary.underserved_note: The China trial included limited English or non-English, low health literacy, rural, older adult, and racial or ethnic minority participants. No trial included Medicaid or safety-net populations in the United States. The UK and German trials reported no underserved subgroups, so there is little basis for judging whether instructions work for low-literacy or limited English proficiency users in American care settings.
